**Important note:** consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics and
pragmatic ethics are four ways of judging whether an action is right.
Of these, ms4ds describes the first three, and says that they
"are not mutually exclusive or exhaustive, so we do not have to choose
one of them or limit our thinking to using only these ideas." Where I write
"I", the view is mine. You are not expected to share
it, and a well-argued position I think is wrong can still get full
marks.

## Summary

A consequentialist judges an action by what it brings about.
Utilitarianism, the best-known form, adds up the good an action does
for everyone it affects. To say what an action brings about, you have
to compare what would happen if it were taken with what would happen if
it were not. That is a causal claim. Data show what happened to the
people who took the action, which answers a different question. Large
observational studies found less heart disease among women who took
hormone therapy after the menopause, and a randomized trial then found
more.

A causal model writes down which variables affect which, and comes
with a rule for working out what an intervention would do. With a
model in hand, an observed difference can sometimes be turned into an
estimate of an effect, by adjusting for the right variables. Which
variables are the right ones depends on the model. You cannot read the
model off the data, so you have to choose one and defend it.

To choose between treating everyone and treating no one, a utilitarian
needs only the average effect times the number of people, provided that
well-being adds up across people and nobody's outcome depends on anyone
else's treatment. That total does not say who gains and who loses. In
reinforcement learning an agent learns a policy, a rule for acting,
that earns a large reward, and the reward is not the same as the good
the policy does: a job center judged on its placement rate does best by
sending people who would have found work anyway.

```{r setup, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
theme_set(theme_minimal())
set.seed(313)
# cividis: viridisLite::cividis(9)[c(1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9)]
navy <- "#00204D"; slate <- "#414D6B"; cgray <- "#7C7B78"; khaki <- "#9B9477"; gold <- "#BCAF6F"; yellow <- "#FFEA46"
two <- c(navy, gold)               # the two groups, wherever there are two

# Causal graphs. Nodes are letters in circles, or words in boxes (boxes = TRUE).
# A node's size is fixed on the page, in inches, while the figure's size decides how
# many inches a data unit is. draw_dag measures both on the graphics device open when it
# is called (in a rendered document, the chunk's figure) and stops every arrow `gap`
# inches short of the two nodes it joins. Arrows listed in `dashed` are dashed (an
# unobserved variable's influence); arrows listed in `highlight` are gold.
# One panel per value of `panel`; `extra` takes theme settings that change the layout,
# such as the panel titles' margins, so that they are measured too.
draw_dag <- function(nodes, edges, dashed = character(0), highlight = character(0), boxes = FALSE,
                     text_size = 4.5, xlim = c(-0.5, 2.5), ylim = c(-0.4, 1.4), extra = theme(),
                     gap = 0.05) {
  if (!"panel" %in% names(nodes)) { nodes$panel <- ""; edges$panel <- "" }
  pad <- unit(0.3, "lines"); border <- 0.25; dot <- 10; stroke <- 0.5; lw <- c(black = 0.5, gold = 1.1)
  p <- ggplot() +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 11), panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")) +
    extra
  p <- if (boxes) {
    p + geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = name), size = text_size, label.size = border,
                   label.padding = pad)
  } else {
    p + geom_point(data = nodes, aes(x, y), size = dot, shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = stroke) +
      geom_text(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = name), size = text_size, parse = TRUE)
  }
  # Inches per data unit: the panels share what the strips and spacing leave of the figure.
  inch <- function(u, f) f(u, "in", valueOnly = TRUE)
  g <- ggplotGrob(p)
  pp <- ggplot_build(p)$layout$panel_params[[1]]
  per_unit <- min((dev.size("in")[1] - sum(inch(g$widths, grid::convertWidth))) /
                    (length(unique(nodes$panel)) * diff(pp$x.range)),
                  (dev.size("in")[2] - sum(inch(g$heights, grid::convertHeight))) / diff(pp$y.range))
  # Half the width and half the height of each node, outline included, in data units.
  if (boxes) {
    text <- lapply(as.character(nodes$name), grid::textGrob, gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = text_size * .pt))
    nodes$hw <- (sapply(text, \(t) inch(grid::grobWidth(t), grid::convertWidth)) / 2 +
                   inch(pad, grid::convertWidth) + border * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit
    nodes$hh <- (sapply(text, \(t) inch(grid::grobHeight(t), grid::convertHeight)) / 2 +
                   inch(pad, grid::convertHeight) + border * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit
  } else {
    # R draws a circle of radius 0.375 times its font size (shape 21)
    nodes$hw <- nodes$hh <- (0.375 * (dot * .pt + stroke * .stroke / 2) / 72 +
                               stroke * .stroke / 2 / 96 / 2) / per_unit
  }
  e <- edges |>
    left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", "from" = "name")) |>
    rename(x0 = x, y0 = y, hw0 = hw, hh0 = hh) |>
    left_join(nodes, by = c("panel", "to" = "name")) |>
    mutate(dx = x - x0, dy = y - y0, len = sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2), ux = dx / len, uy = dy / len,
           col = ifelse(paste(from, to) %in% highlight, "#BCAF6F", "black"),
           style = ifelse(paste(from, to) %in% dashed, "dashed", "solid"),
           # the start clears the node by gap; the end by gap and half the arrow's line width,
           # which the rounded tip adds
           g0 = gap / per_unit,
           g1 = (gap + ifelse(col == "black", lw[["black"]], lw[["gold"]]) * .pt / 96 / 2) / per_unit,
           # distance from a node's center, along the arrow, to the node's outline grown by g
           s0 = if (boxes) pmin((hw0 + g0) / pmax(abs(ux), 1e-9), (hh0 + g0) / pmax(abs(uy), 1e-9)) else hw0 + g0,
           s1 = if (boxes) pmin((hw + g1) / pmax(abs(ux), 1e-9), (hh + g1) / pmax(abs(uy), 1e-9)) else hw + g1,
           xs = x0 + s0 * ux, ys = y0 + s0 * uy, xe = x - s1 * ux, ye = y - s1 * uy)
  p + geom_segment(data = e, aes(x = xs, y = ys, xend = xe, yend = ye, linetype = style, color = col),
                   arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed"),
                   linewidth = ifelse(e$col == "black", lw[["black"]], lw[["gold"]]), show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_linetype_identity() + scale_color_identity()
}

# Labels with math letters. In `label`, the text between dollar signs is drawn in
# MathJax_Math, the TeX italic of an older MathJax, which looks like the italic of the
# slides' formulas; the rest is drawn in the device's default font. The pieces are placed
# when the plot is drawn, so they stay together at any figure size. A label cannot hold a
# literal dollar sign, and hjust and vjust are numbers. `nudge_y` moves the labels up by
# that many points (y = Inf is the top of the panel).
GeomMathText <- ggproto("GeomMathText", Geom,
  required_aes = c("x", "y", "label"),
  default_aes = aes(colour = "black", size = 6, hjust = 0.5, vjust = 0.5),
  draw_key = draw_key_text,
  draw_panel = function(data, panel_params, coord, nudge_y = 0) {
    data <- coord$transform(data, panel_params)
    labels <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(data)), function(i) {
      d <- data[i, ]
      parts <- strsplit(as.character(d$label), "$", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
      math <- seq_along(parts) %% 2 == 0
      keep <- nzchar(parts)
      if (!any(keep)) return(grid::nullGrob())
      # math pieces also ask for italic, so that they stay italic if the font is missing
      font <- function(m) grid::gpar(col = d$colour, fontsize = d$size * .pt,
                                     fontfamily = if (m) "MathJax_Math" else "",
                                     fontface = if (m) "italic" else "plain")
      pieces <- unname(Map(function(p, m) grid::textGrob(p, gp = font(m)), parts[keep], math[keep]))
      widths <- lapply(pieces, grid::grobWidth)
      x <- unit(d$x, "native") - d$hjust * Reduce(`+`, widths)
      # one baseline for all the pieces, placed by the height of the default font's capitals
      y <- unit(d$y, "native") + unit(nudge_y, "pt") -
        d$vjust * grid::grobHeight(grid::textGrob("M", gp = font(FALSE)))
      for (k in seq_along(pieces)) {
        pieces[[k]] <- grid::editGrob(pieces[[k]], x = x, y = y, just = c("left", "bottom"))
        x <- x + widths[[k]]
      }
      grid::gTree(children = do.call(grid::gList, pieces))
    })
    grid::gTree(children = do.call(grid::gList, labels))
  }
)
geom_mathtext <- function(mapping = NULL, data = NULL, ...) {
  layer(geom = GeomMathText, mapping = mapping, data = data, stat = "identity",
        position = "identity", show.legend = FALSE, inherit.aes = FALSE, params = list(...))
}
# The math letters and pi in the figures are drawn in MathJax_Math. Stop if it is missing,
# rather than draw them in another font without saying so.
if (requireNamespace("systemfonts", quietly = TRUE) &&
    !"MathJax_Math" %in% systemfonts::system_fonts()$family) {
  stop("The font MathJax_Math is not installed. It draws the math letters in this file's ",
       "figures (on Debian or Ubuntu: apt-get install fonts-mathjax).")
}
```

## Normative ethics: four frameworks

Consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics are in
[ms4ds, section 3.2](https://joshualoftus.com/ms4ds/ethical-data-science.html#philosophy-of-ethics),
and all four are in the Wikipedia articles on
[consequentialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequentialism),
[deontology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deontology),
[virtue ethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtue_ethics) and
[pragmatic ethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pragmatic_ethics).

**Consequentialism** judges an action by its effects. Its best-known
form is utilitarianism. Of the difficulties ms4ds lists, the one this
course can help with is "uncertainty about predicting consequences."

**Deontology** judges an action by whether it follows a rule or a duty,
"rather than based on the consequences of the action," in Wikipedia's
words. An action can be right though its consequences are bad, if it
kept to the rule. Provided you know which rules you have a duty to
follow, you may not need to predict consequences at all, which makes
deontology simpler to apply. If a rule can never be overridden, though,
you may be bound to it when following it leads somewhere terrible.
Kant is the best-known deontologist.

**Virtue ethics** judges character. In Wikipedia's words, it
"prioritizes the development of moral character and dispositions (good
habits)." A person acting
honestly or courageously can be acting well even when a rule was broken
and the outcome was bad. Virtues can conflict, and people do not agree
on which traits are virtues.

**Pragmatic ethics** treats moral norms the way a scientist treats a
hypothesis. A scientist can accept a hypothesis and work with it as if
it were true, while expecting later work to refine or replace it. Ethical pragmatists think that "norms, principles, and
moral criteria are likely to be improved as a result of inquiry."
They hold that it can be appropriate to work within any of the other
three frameworks, while leaving room to move beyond it. One image for
this is Neurath's boat, which likens the gradual change of ethical
norms to sailors rebuilding their ship while at sea. One criticism is
that pragmatic ethics describes how people do make moral judgments
rather than how they should.

I have argued for a pragmatism about models, statistical and causal
([Loftus 2024](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/loftus24a.html)):
"Instead of asking if a model is right, correct, or accurate, we should
ask if it is useful for a certain purpose." In the same paper I borrow
a distinction from Tukey (1960), one of this week's optional readings.
Conclusions should be final and well tested, so it makes sense to hold
them to high standards of evidence. Decisions are temporary. We make
them so that we can act, and we expect that we may need to try
something else. You can decide to use a causal model without taking
the model as conclusive.

### Utilitarianism

Utilitarianism is the consequentialism of Jeremy Bentham, regarded as
its founder, and John Stuart Mill. It says to choose the action that
does the greatest good for the greatest number of people. In its
classical form the good is happiness, and what matters, in the
Wikipedia article's words, is "to aggregate happiness; the happiness of
everyone, and not the happiness of any particular person." Later
utilitarians measure the good in other ways, for instance by how far
people's preferences are satisfied.

ms4ds lists four difficulties:

- Defining utility. Someone has to say what counts as good and how to
  measure it. In data science this is the choice of an outcome, a
  metric or a loss function, and the first of the five lenses asks
  about it: what are we optimizing or predicting?
- Trading off one person's good against another's. A total or an
  average lets a gain to one person make up for a loss to another. The
  average treatment effect, later in these notes, is an average of this
  kind.
- Judging single acts or general rules. Act utilitarianism judges each
  action by its consequences. Rule utilitarianism judges a rule by the
  consequences of following it, and an act by whether it follows a good
  rule. A model that makes thousands of decisions is a rule.
- Predicting consequences. In ms4ds's words, "The last issue,
  predicting consequences, is one where the intersection with data
  science is particularly relevant."

Data science, ms4ds says, "is usually framed (perhaps implicitly) as
utilitarian because of its focus on prediction/causation
(consequences) and optimization (utility)." A recommender that ranks
items to raise average engagement, a lender's model that approves loans
to maximize expected profit, and an A/B test that keeps whichever
version has the higher mean of some metric each add up a quantity over
people and choose the action with the larger total. Each is utilitarian
in form. Whether the quantity is anyone's good is the first difficulty
again: a lender's profit is not its borrowers' happiness. A
deontologist asks of the same systems whether the people in the A/B
test agreed to be experimented on, and whether anyone is treated in a
way that no gain to others could justify. A virtue ethicist asks what
building such a system says about the people who build it.

## Applied ethics: the Belmont and Menlo principles

```{r belmont_timeline, echo=FALSE, fig.height=1.8, fig.width=7, fig.alt="A timeline. A dark bar marks the Tuskegee study, 1932 to 1972; dots mark the National Research Act in 1974, the Belmont Report in 1978 (respect for persons, beneficence, justice) and the Menlo Report in 2012 (adds respect for law and the public interest)."}
lab <- data.frame(
  x     = c(1975.5, 1976.5, 1976.5, 2013.5, 2013.5),
  y     = c(0.3, -0.3, -0.68, 0.86, 0.3),
  label = c("1974 National Research Act", "1978 Belmont Report", "respect for persons, beneficence, justice",
            "2012 Menlo Report", "adds respect for law\nand the public interest"),
  hj    = c(1, 0, 0, 1, 1), vj = c(0, 1, 1, 0, 0),
  bold  = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE))
ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = 1928, xend = 2018, y = 0, yend = 0, color = cgray, linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 1932, xmax = 1972, ymin = -0.17, ymax = 0.17, fill = navy) +
  annotate("text", x = 1952, y = 0, label = "Tuskegee study, 1932 to 1972", color = "white", size = 3.9) +
  annotate("point", x = c(1974, 1978, 2012), y = 0, size = 3.4, color = gold) +
  geom_text(data = lab, aes(x, y, label = label, hjust = hj, vjust = vj,
                            fontface = ifelse(bold, "bold", "plain"), color = ifelse(bold, navy, "black")),
            size = 3.7, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_color_identity() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1928, 2018), ylim = c(-1.05, 1.35), clip = "off") +
  theme_void()
```

From 1932 the United States Public Health Service ran a study in which
African American men in Alabama were recruited with the promise of free
health care. Most of them had syphilis. They were never told that they
had it, or that they were not being treated, and they were kept from
penicillin after it was known to be an effective treatment.
[ms4ds, section 3.3](https://joshualoftus.com/ms4ds/ethical-data-science.html#applied-ethics),
tells the story of the Tuskegee study. It ended in 1972, after a
whistleblower came forward and newspapers took up the story. Prompted
in part by it, the National Research Act of 1974 created a national
commission for the protection of research subjects. The commission's
report, released in 1978, is the
[Belmont Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Report), named
after the conference center in Elkridge, Maryland, where part of it was
drafted. It sets out three principles: respect for persons, beneficence
and justice. In 2012 the Menlo Report, from
the US Department of Homeland Security, adapted them for cybersecurity
research and added a fourth. Together they are the
**Belmont--Menlo principles**, here in the Menlo Report's wording, which
ms4ds quotes:

- Respect for persons: "Participation as a research subject is
  voluntary, and follows from informed consent; Treat individuals as
  autonomous agents and respect their right to determine their own best
  interests; ..."
- Beneficence: "Do not harm; Maximize probable benefits and minimize
  probable harms; Systematically assess both risk of harm and benefit."
- Justice: "Each person deserves equal consideration in how to be
  treated, and the benefits of research should be fairly distributed
  ...; Selection of subjects should be fair, and burdens should be
  allocated equitably across impacted subjects."
- Respect for law and the public interest: "Engage in legal due
  diligence; Be transparent in methods and results; Be accountable for
  actions."

Applied ethics does not pick one of the four frameworks. Respect for
persons reads like a deontological rule, and beneficence like a
consequentialist one. To maximize probable benefits you have to predict
what a study, or a product, will do to the people it touches.

### The five Cs

[ms4ds, section 3.3.2](https://joshualoftus.com/ms4ds/ethical-data-science.html#the-five-cs-framework)
summarizes a practical framework for data work from Loukides, Mason
and Patil's book *Ethics and Data Science*, the five Cs:

- Consent: data are collected only from people who explicitly agreed,
  knowing what would be collected and what it may be used for. Informed
  consent is part of Belmont's respect for persons.
- Clarity: people should understand what their consent allows, which
  user agreements often make hard, even for well-informed readers.
- Consistency and trust: when a system behaves consistently, people can
  predict what it will do and decide whether to trust it. Many
  controversies in data science began with behavior people did not
  expect.
- Control and transparency: after consenting, people should still be
  able to see the status of their data and opt in or out of particular
  uses.
- Consequences: the unintended consequences of some kinds of data
  existing should be anticipated. Children, and sensitive data such as
  genome sequences, may need extra protection, and combining sources can
  re-identify people.

## The consequentialist's problem

Wikipedia states the consequentialist position like this: an act is
right "if and only if the act (or in some views, the rule under which it
falls) will produce, will probably produce, or is intended to produce,
a greater balance of good over evil than any available alternative."
That is a comparison between actions. Only one of them is taken, so at
most one of the outcomes is ever seen. The others are what would have
happened, and a claim about what would have happened is a causal claim.
A consequentialist cannot state their own position on an action
without a causal model, because the consequences of an action are its
causal effects.
In [ms4ds, section 3.4](https://joshualoftus.com/ms4ds/ethical-data-science.html#causality-and-ethics):
"Causal understanding is necessary to apply consequentialism. An
observational model of the world does not tell us what consequences we
can expect to result from any action which is an intervention."

```{r alternatives, echo=FALSE, fig.height=1.9, fig.width=7, fig.alt="A choice branches into the action taken, whose consequences are seen, and an alternative, drawn dashed, whose consequences are never seen."}
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("choice", "action taken", "alternative", "consequences seen", "never seen"),
                    x = c(0, 1.9, 1.9, 4.2, 4.2), y = c(0.5, 1, 0, 1, 0)),
         data.frame(from = c("choice", "choice", "action taken", "alternative"),
                    to = c("action taken", "alternative", "consequences seen", "never seen")),
         dashed = c("choice alternative", "alternative never seen"),
         boxes = TRUE, xlim = c(-0.8, 5.3), ylim = c(-0.3, 1.3))
```

In ms4ds's example, observational data show couples happier after
divorcing. That does not tell a utilitarian that everyone who can
should divorce: couples who divorce were probably unhappy together,
and other couples may not be.

Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan open their chapter on causality, on the
page before this week's reading starts, with a pair of questions. The
first is "Do 16 year-old drivers have a higher incidence rate of traffic
accidents than 18 year-old drivers?" That is a difference between two
conditional probabilities, and a large enough sample answers it. The
second is "Would traffic fatalities decrease if we raised the legal
driving age by two years?" It asks for "the effect of a hypothetical
action," and the same sample does not answer it. Older drivers also
have more driving experience. The authors add that 18-year-olds who
started driving late may be unusually cautious, or live where people
need a car less.

How often do researchers move from what happened to what should be
done? Prasad, Jorgenson, Ioannidis and Cifu (2013) read the 631
original articles published in 2010 in four leading medical journals,
and found 298 eligible observational studies. In 167 of the 298 (56%),
the authors recommended a medical practice on the strength of their
results. Only 24 of those 167 said that a
randomized trial should be done first.

```{r prasad, echo=FALSE, fig.height=1.8, fig.width=7, fig.alt="Bars: 298 observational studies; 167 of them recommended a medical practice; 24 of those said a randomized trial should come first."}
prasad <- data.frame(label = c("observational studies", "recommended a practice", "of those, asked for a trial first"),
                     n = c(298, 167, 24))
prasad$label <- factor(prasad$label, levels = rev(prasad$label))
ggplot(prasad, aes(n, label, fill = label)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.25, size = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(c(cgray, gold, navy), levels(prasad$label)[3:1])) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 340), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11))
```

### Hormone therapy and heart disease

In 1996 the Nurses' Health Study reported on 59,337 women followed for
up to 16 years. Women who took estrogen with progestin after the
menopause, compared with women who did not use hormones, had "a marked
decrease in the risk of major coronary heart disease": a relative risk
of 0.39 (95% confidence interval 0.19 to 0.78), adjusted for the
confounding variables the authors measured. They concluded that adding
progestin "does not appear to attenuate the cardioprotective effects of
postmenopausal estrogen therapy." A protective effect is a claim about
what taking the hormones does.

The Women's Health Initiative tested the claim. It randomized 16,608
women aged 50 to 79, all with a uterus, to estrogen with progestin or to
a placebo, and it
was stopped early, after a mean of 5.2 years, because of an excess of
invasive breast cancer and an overall balance of risks over benefits.
For coronary heart disease the hazard ratio was 1.29, with a nominal
95% interval of 1.02 to 1.63; in absolute terms, about 7 more cases per
10,000 person-years. Nominal means that the interval was computed as if this
were the only outcome and the only analysis, though the trial tracked
many outcomes and was analyzed repeatedly as it ran. Its conclusion was about
action: the regimen "should not be initiated or continued for primary
prevention" of coronary heart disease.

```{r hrt, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.2}
hrt <- data.frame(
  label = c("Nurses' Health Study, 1996\nestrogen with progestin against no hormones",
            "Women's Health Initiative trial, 2002\nassigned to treatment against placebo",
            "Nurses' Health Study analyzed like the trial, 2008\nstarters against non-starters, first two years",
            "the same, whole follow-up"),
  est = c(0.39, 1.29, 1.42, 0.96), lo = c(0.19, 1.02, 0.92, 0.78), hi = c(0.78, 1.63, 2.20, 1.18),
  design = c("observational", "randomized", "observational", "observational"))
hrt$label <- factor(hrt$label, levels = rev(hrt$label))
ggplot(hrt, aes(est, label, color = design)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = cgray) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(observational = gold, randomized = navy)) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.2, 0.5, 1, 2), limits = c(0.18, 2.4)) +
  labs(x = "relative risk or hazard ratio, coronary heart disease (log scale)", y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))
```

Two explanations were offered, and both can be true. One is
confounding: the women who chose hormones differed from the women who
did not, in ways that also affect the heart. This week's reading uses
the case as its example of confounding: "a suspected beneficial effect
of hormone replacement therapy in reducing cardiovascular disease
disappeared after identifying socioeconomic status as a confounding
variable." The review it cites (Humphrey, Chan and Sox 2002) pooled
earlier studies. Among those that had adjusted for socioeconomic status
and the major risk factors for coronary disease, the summary relative
risk of coronary disease with any hormone use was 1.07 (credible
interval 0.79 to 1.48).

```{r hrt_dag, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.2, fig.width=7}
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("socioeconomic status", "age", "hormone use", "heart disease"),
                    x = c(0, 2.7, 0, 2.7), y = c(1, 1, 0, 0)),
         data.frame(from = c("socioeconomic status", "socioeconomic status", "age", "age", "hormone use"),
                    to = c("hormone use", "heart disease", "hormone use", "heart disease", "heart disease")),
         highlight = "hormone use heart disease", boxes = TRUE, xlim = c(-1.2, 3.9), ylim = c(-0.25, 1.25))
```

The gold arrow is the claim that the hormones protect the heart. The
four black arrows can produce a difference between users and non-users
without it.

The other explanation is the comparison itself. Hernán and colleagues
(2008) went back to the Nurses' Health Study and analyzed it the way
the trial was analyzed: women who started estrogen with progestin
against women who did not start, both followed from the same point.
Over the first two years the hazard ratio was 1.42 (0.92 to 2.20), and
over the whole follow-up 0.96 (0.78 to 1.18), estimates they describe
as "similar to those from the Women's Health Initiative." The
differences that remained, they suggest, "could be largely explained by
differences in the distribution of time since menopause and length of
follow-up."

The same cohort gave 0.39 under one comparison, and between 0.96 and
1.42 under another, analyzed differently. A doctor deciding whether a patient should start
hormones is choosing an action. The comparison that matches it is
women who started against women who did not, from the same day. Women
who took hormones against women who did not is a comparison of two
groups of people, and it answers a question about them.

## Causal models

The reading builds a model as a program. A **structural causal model**
is "a sequence of assignments for generating a joint distribution
starting from independent noise variables." Each variable is assigned
as a function of some of the variables before it, its *parents*, and of
its own noise. The **causal graph** has a node for each variable and an
arrow into it from each of its parents. Three shapes come up over and
over. The letters are the ones this course uses.

```{r three_shapes, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.4, fig.width=8}
shapes <- c("fork: Z is a common cause", "chain: M is a mediator", "collider: C is a common effect")
nodes <- data.frame(panel = rep(shapes, each = 3),
                    name = c("Z", "X", "Y", "M", "X", "Y", "C", "X", "Y"),
                    x = rep(c(1, 0, 2), 3), y = rep(c(1, 0, 0), 3))
edges <- data.frame(panel = rep(shapes, each = 2),
                    from = c("Z", "Z", "X", "M", "X", "Y"),
                    to = c("X", "Y", "M", "Y", "C", "C"))
nodes$panel <- factor(nodes$panel, levels = shapes); edges$panel <- factor(edges$panel, levels = shapes)
draw_dag(nodes, edges)
```

In a **fork**, $Z$ has arrows to both $X$ and $Y$: it is a common
cause. In a **chain**, $X \to M \to Y$, the **mediator** $M$ is one of
the routes by which $X$ affects $Y$. In a **collider**, $X$ and $Y$
both have arrows into $C$: it is a common effect. A common cause is
the usual source of confounding.

### Conditioning and intervening

Take the reading's first program. Whether a person exercises, $X$, is
a coin toss with probability $1/2$. Without exercise, a person becomes
overweight ($W = 1$) with probability $1/3$ and develops heart disease
($H = 1$) with probability $1/3$, independently. Exercise prevents
both:
$$
X := U_1, \qquad
W := \begin{cases} 0 & X = 1 \\ U_2 & X = 0 \end{cases}, \qquad
H := \begin{cases} 0 & X = 1 \\ U_3 & X = 0 \end{cases},
$$
with $U_1 \sim \mathrm{Ber}(1/2)$ and $U_2, U_3 \sim \mathrm{Ber}(1/3)$
independent, where $\mathrm{Ber}(q)$ is 1 with probability $q$ and 0
otherwise. (The reading writes $B(q)$.) The graph is a
fork, $W \leftarrow X \to H$.

The probability of heart disease is
$P(H = 1) = P(X = 0)\,P(U_3 = 1) = \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac13 = \tfrac16$.
Now observe that someone is overweight. That happens only without
exercise, so $X = 0$, and
$$
P(H = 1 \mid W = 1) = \tfrac13 .
$$
Overweight people have twice the rate of heart disease of the
population as a whole, $1/3$ against $1/6$. Would a program
that changed people's weight change their heart disease? Changing
weight is an action on $W$. In the program it means replacing the line
that assigns $W$ by a constant, $W := 1$ or $W := 0$, and leaving every
other line alone. In the graph, that deletes the arrow into $W$ and
keeps the arrow from $X$ to $H$.

```{r program_do, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.2, fig.width=6}
pp <- c("the program", "after do(W := 1)")
nodes <- data.frame(panel = rep(pp, each = 3), name = rep(c("X", "W", "H"), 2),
                    x = rep(c(1, 0, 2), 2), y = rep(c(1, 0, 0), 2))
edges <- data.frame(panel = c(pp[1], pp[1], pp[2]), from = "X", to = c("W", "H", "H"))
nodes$panel <- factor(nodes$panel, levels = pp); edges$panel <- factor(edges$panel, levels = pp)
draw_dag(nodes, edges, extra = theme(strip.clip = "off", strip.text = element_text(size = 11, margin = margin(t = 2, b = 6))))
```

Do that, and $H$ still depends only on $X$ and $U_3$:
$$
P(H = 1 \mid do(W := 1)) = \tfrac16 = P(H = 1 \mid do(W := 0)).
$$
Setting the weight does nothing to the heart. Observing the weight told
you about the exercise, and the exercise is what affects the heart.

The reading's second program reverses one arrow: weight drives
exercise, $W \to X \to H$. Overweight people exercise with probability
$1/2$ and nobody else does. There, conditioning on $W = 1$ and setting
$W := 1$ both give $1/6$, so the two can agree. Whether they do depends
on the graph.

$P(Y \mid X = x)$ describes the people whose $X$ happened to be $x$.
$P(Y \mid do(X := x))$ describes what would happen if $X$ were set to
$x$ for everyone, which in the graph means deleting every arrow into
$X$ and fixing its value. The reading's definition: "We say that $X$
and $Y$ are **confounded** when the causal effect of action $X := x$ on
$Y$ does not coincide with the corresponding conditional probability."

### The average treatment effect

For a binary $X$, the **average treatment effect** is
$$
\text{ATE} = E[Y \mid do(X := 1)] - E[Y \mid do(X := 0)],
$$
the difference in the mean of $Y$ between a world where everyone is
treated and one where nobody is. Each term deletes the arrows into $X$
and sets $X$ to the same value for everyone. "Causal effects are
population quantities," as the reading says. The effect on one person,
or on one group, can differ from it. "This policy causes better
outcomes" is a statement about a quantity like this one. The observed
difference $E[Y \mid X = 1] - E[Y \mid X = 0]$ is a statement about who
happened to be treated.

Suppose $Y$ measures how well off a person is, on a scale on which
gains and losses can be added across people, and nobody's outcome
depends on anyone else's treatment. Then treating all $n$ people in a
population rather than none changes the expected total of $Y$ by
$n \times \text{ATE}$. That is the comparison a utilitarian makes
between those two actions, and it needs nothing else. In the total a
gain to one person offsets a loss to another, so a positive average
treatment effect is consistent with some people being made worse off.
Justice, the third Belmont principle, concerns who receives the
benefits of research and who bears its burdens. Asked of a policy, the
same question is not answered by the average. Effects within groups say more,
and a trial can estimate them for groups defined by what was known
before treatment. The effect on one person is never observed, because
each person is either treated or not. If it could be, ten people might
look like the bars below: an average effect of 1 and a total of 10,
with three people made worse off.

```{r gains, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2, fig.width=6, fig.alt="Bars for ten imagined people: seven gain between 1 and 4, three lose between 1 and 3; a dashed line marks the average, 1."}
gains <- data.frame(person = factor(1:10), effect = c(4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, -1, -2, -3))
ggplot(gains, aes(person, effect, fill = effect > 0)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = cgray) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(gains$effect), linetype = "dashed", color = navy) +
  annotate("text", x = 10.45, y = 1.6, label = "ATE = 1", hjust = 1, color = navy, size = 3.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = gold, `FALSE` = slate)) +
  labs(x = "ten imagined people", y = "gain") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_blank())
```

### Prediction and intervention

Figure 1 of [my 2024 paper](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/loftus24a.html)
has three graphs, redrawn here.

```{r three_dags, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.4, fig.width=8}
pics <- c("X causes Y", "Y causes X", "Z causes both")
nodes <- data.frame(panel = c(pics[1], pics[1], pics[2], pics[2], pics[3], pics[3], pics[3]),
                    name = c("X", "Y", "X", "Y", "Z", "X", "Y"),
                    x = c(0, 2, 0, 2, 1, 0, 2), y = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0))
edges <- data.frame(panel = c(pics[1], pics[2], pics[3], pics[3]),
                    from = c("X", "Y", "Z", "Z"), to = c("Y", "X", "X", "Y"))
nodes$panel <- factor(nodes$panel, levels = pics); edges$panel <- factor(edges$panel, levels = pics)
draw_dag(nodes, edges)
```

Its caption ends: "It is possible that the accuracy of some function
$f(X)$ in predicting $Y$ is equal in all cases." A policy that changes $X$ in order to
change $Y$ works only in the first. Under the other two, setting $X$
leaves $Y$ alone; to change $Y$ you would act on $Y$ or on its causes,
which in the third include $Z$.
"If we expect a model to also tell us what happens when we intervene on
variables, then [...] models with equal predictive accuracy are no
longer equivalent. We become responsible to choose one of them."

## Confounding and adjustment

Say you want to argue that a job-search course for people out of work
should be expanded, because the people who took it were more often in
work six months later. In a version with numbers chosen to work by
hand, a thousand people are registered with a job center, which refers
some of them to the course. It refers people who worked in the previous
year more readily, because it judges them ready. In this version
everyone referred attends and nobody else does, so referral and
attendance are the same. Write $Z = 1$ for worked in the previous year,
$X = 1$ for attended the course, and $Y = 1$ for in work six months
later.

| | attended ($X = 1$) | did not attend ($X = 0$) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| worked last year ($Z = 1$), 500 people | 280 of 400 in work (70%) | 60 of 100 in work (60%) |
| did not ($Z = 0$), 500 people | 40 of 100 in work (40%) | 120 of 400 in work (30%) |
| total, 1,000 people | 320 of 500 in work (64%) | 180 of 500 in work (36%) |

Of the people who attended, 64% are in work, against 36% of those who
did not. A press release would say the course raises employment by 28
percentage points. Now read the rows. Among people who worked last
year, 70% of attenders are in work against 60% of the others. Among
people who did not, 40% against 30%. Within each row the difference is
10 points.

The numbers came from this graph:

```{r course_dag, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.4, fig.width=3}
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("Z", "X", "Y"), x = c(1, 0, 2), y = c(1, 0, 0)),
         data.frame(from = c("Z", "Z", "X"), to = c("X", "Y", "Y")))
```

$Z$ pushes people onto the course: 80% of those who worked last year
attend, against 20% of the others. $Z$ also makes people more
employable, whether or not they attend. Attenders are in work more
often partly because of the course and partly because of who was sent.
The 28 points mixes the two.

### The adjustment formula

Intervening on $X$ deletes the arrow $Z \to X$. Everyone attends, or
nobody does, and $Z$ keeps the distribution it had. So the mean outcome
under $do(X := 1)$ is the within-row rate for attenders, averaged over
the rows with weights given by how common each row is:
$$
\begin{aligned}
E[Y \mid do(X := 1)] &= \sum_z E[Y \mid X = 1, Z = z]\, P(Z = z) \\
&= 0.7 \times 0.5 + 0.4 \times 0.5 = 0.55 .
\end{aligned}
$$
Likewise $E[Y \mid do(X := 0)] = 0.6 \times 0.5 + 0.3 \times 0.5 = 0.45$,
and the average treatment effect is $0.10$. In general,
$$
\boxed{\;P(Y = y \mid do(X := x)) = \sum_z P(Y = y \mid X = x, Z = z)\, P(Z = z)\;}
$$
when $Z$ satisfies the backdoor criterion below, and every value of $Z$
that occurs includes some people with $X = x$ (otherwise
$P(Y = y \mid X = x, Z = z)$ is not defined). This is the
**adjustment formula**. The reading writes it with the parents of $X$
in place of $Z$, and calls computing it "controlling for" a set of
variables: estimate the effect "separately in every slice of the
population defined by a condition $Z = z$," then average the slices,
each weighted by its share of the population.

The observed comparison weights the rows differently. It weights each
row by its share of the people who attended, or of the people who did
not:
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) &= \frac{0.7 \times 400 + 0.4 \times 100}{500} = 0.64, \\
P(Y = 1 \mid X = 0) &= \frac{0.6 \times 100 + 0.3 \times 400}{500} = 0.36 .
\end{aligned}
$$
The attenders come mostly from the $Z = 1$ row and the others mostly
from the $Z = 0$ row, and the two rows have different rates of being
in work whatever people do. The extra 18 points come from the referral
policy sending to the course the people who would more often find work
anyway.

### Randomization

Suppose the center had referred people at random, half of each row,
and as before everyone referred had attended. Then attenders would
come half from each row, and so would the others. The shares in work
to expect are
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) &= 0.5 \times 0.7 + 0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.55, \\
P(Y = 1 \mid X = 0) &= 0.5 \times 0.6 + 0.5 \times 0.3 = 0.45 .
\end{aligned}
$$
The difference to expect is now $0.55 - 0.45 = 0.10$, the average
treatment effect. The difference observed after any one randomization
is near $0.10$, and it varies from one draw to the next because each
draw sends different people to the course. Randomizing deletes the
arrow into $X$ in the world itself, so the comparison to expect and the
interventional one coincide. In the reading's words, "the goal of a
randomized controlled trial is to break natural inclination."
Randomization also deletes arrows from variables nobody measured, which
adjustment cannot do.

In practice some people offered a course do not take it, and some
people not offered it find one elsewhere. Randomizing the offer then
gives the effect of the offer, not of attending. A trial's *arms* are
the groups people were assigned to, and a comparison by arm, whatever
each person then did, is an **intention-to-treat analysis**. The
hormone trial's main analysis was of this kind, and it is the analysis
Hernán and colleagues emulated.

### The backdoor criterion

A *backdoor path* from $X$ to $Y$ is a path between them that starts
with an arrow into $X$. In the course example there is one,
$X \leftarrow Z \to Y$. In the standard statement, which the reading
cites to Pearl, a set of variables $Z$ satisfies the
**backdoor criterion** for the effect of $X$ on $Y$ if

1. no variable in $Z$ is a descendant of $X$, and
2. $Z$ blocks every backdoor path from $X$ to $Y$.

A path through a fork or a chain is blocked by conditioning on the
variable in the middle. Colliders work differently, as the reading
explains; none of the backdoor paths in these notes goes through one.
When $Z$ satisfies the criterion, the adjustment formula with that $Z$
gives $P(Y = y \mid do(X := x))$.

The first condition says what not to adjust for. A mediator $M$ on
$X \to M \to Y$ is a descendant of $X$. Adjusting for it removes the
part of the effect that runs through $M$. What is left is not the
total effect, which is what a decision to change $X$ needs. If nothing
else affects both $M$ and $Y$, it is the direct effect, the part that
does not pass through $M$. The reading lists three cases: controlling
for a
confounder removes confounding, and controlling for a mediator "will
eliminate some of the causal influence of $X$ on $Y$." Its third case
is the collider. So "control for everything you measured" is not a
safe default. You decide which variables to hold fixed from the graph,
and someone has to draw the graph.

### Optional: Berkeley, 1973

The reading starts from the 1973 admissions to graduate programs at the
University of California, Berkeley: 44% of the 8,442 men who applied were
admitted, and 35% of the 4,321 women. In the six largest departments,
which R has as `UCBAdmissions`, 44.5% of 2,691 men and 30.4% of 1,835
women were admitted. Department by department the comparison goes the
other way in four of the six.

```{r berkeley, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.4}
ucb <- as.data.frame(UCBAdmissions) |>
  group_by(Dept, Gender) |>
  summarize(applied = sum(Freq), admitted = sum(Freq[Admit == "Admitted"]), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(rate = admitted / applied, Dept = as.character(Dept))
overall <- as.data.frame(UCBAdmissions) |>
  group_by(Gender) |>
  summarize(applied = sum(Freq), admitted = sum(Freq[Admit == "Admitted"]), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(rate = admitted / applied, Dept = "all six")
bind_rows(ucb, overall) |>
  mutate(Dept = factor(Dept, levels = c("all six", LETTERS[1:6]))) |>
  ggplot(aes(Dept, rate, color = Gender, size = applied)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_manual(values = two, labels = c("men", "women")) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 9, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.9)) +
  labs(x = "department", y = "admitted", color = NULL,
       title = "Six largest departments; point size is the number of applicants")
```

The reading's Table 5.1 has 520 men applying to department B and 60%
admitted, where `UCBAdmissions`, which cites the same 1975 paper, has
560 and 63%. Nothing here depends on the difference.

A reversal like this is called Simpson's paradox. The arithmetic is the
course table's: the overall rates weight each department by who applied
to it, and women applied more often to departments that admitted fewer
applicants. Which comparison is the right one depends on the question
and on the graph. If sex affects which department a person applies to,
and department affects admission, then department is a mediator.
Comparing within departments asks whether women and men who applied to
the same department were treated differently. Comparing overall asks
whether women ended up admitted less often. The reading adds that the
data record nothing about qualifications, and asks why women applied to
the departments they did: perhaps others were unwelcoming. You cannot
tell which story is right from the admissions data.

## Optional: omitted-variable bias

The same argument works for a regression slope. Take a linear
structural causal model with independent, mean-zero noise:
$$
Z := U_Z, \qquad X := \alpha Z + U_X, \qquad Y := \beta X + \gamma Z + U_Y .
$$
The graph is the course graph again: $Z \to X$, $Z \to Y$, $X \to Y$.
Intervening on $X$ deletes the first arrow, so
$E[Y \mid do(X := x)] = \beta x + \gamma E[Z] = \beta x$, and raising $X$
by one unit raises the mean of $Y$ by $\beta$.

Now regress $Y$ on $X$ alone, as someone with data on $X$ and $Y$ only
would. The population slope is $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$.
Substituting for $Y$,
$$
\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = \beta \operatorname{Var}(X) + \gamma \operatorname{Cov}(X, Z),
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(X, Z) = \alpha \operatorname{Var}(Z),
$$
because $U_Y$ is independent of $X$ and $Z$, and $U_X$ is independent
of $Z$. So
$$
\boxed{\;\begin{aligned}
\text{slope of } Y \text{ on } X &= \beta + \gamma\,\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X, Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)} \\
&= \beta + \gamma \alpha \frac{\operatorname{Var}(Z)}{\alpha^2 \operatorname{Var}(Z) + \operatorname{Var}(U_X)}
\end{aligned}\;}
$$
The second term is the **omitted-variable bias**: $\gamma$, the effect
of the left-out variable on $Y$ with $X$ held fixed (its own arrow into
$Y$), times the slope of the left-out variable on $X$. Its sign is the sign of $\gamma\alpha$, the product of the two
arrows out of $Z$. With $\alpha = \gamma = 1$, $\beta = 0.5$ and both
variances 1, the slope is $0.5 + 1 \times 1 \times 1/2 = 1.0$, double
the effect. With $\beta = 0$ the slope is $0.5$ and the effect is zero.
$X$ predicts $Y$, and intervening on $X$ does nothing: the third graph
in Figure 1, with numbers.

This is a bias. The slope converges to
$\beta + \gamma\alpha \operatorname{Var}(Z)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$ as the
sample grows, so more data gives the same wrong answer with a narrower
interval.

Fitting $Y$ on $X$ and $Z$ together (`lm(Y ~ X + Z)` in R) is a
regression with two predictors. Its coefficient on $X$ is the slope of
$Y$ on the part of $X$ that $Z$ does not predict: regress $X$ on $Z$,
keep the residuals, and regress $Y$ on them. In this model the
regression of $X$ on $Z$ has slope $\alpha$, the residual is $U_X$, and
$$
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y, U_X)}{\operatorname{Var}(U_X)} = \frac{\beta \operatorname{Var}(U_X)}{\operatorname{Var}(U_X)} = \beta ,
$$
because $Z$ and $U_Y$ are independent of $U_X$. So the coefficient on
$X$ converges to $\beta$, the effect. In this linear model that
coefficient is the effect the adjustment formula gives.

```{r ovb_sim}
set.seed(3)
n <- 5000
Z <- rnorm(n)
X <- 1 * Z + rnorm(n)
Y <- 0.5 * X + 1 * Z + rnorm(n)
coef(lm(Y ~ X))["X"]        # Y on X alone
coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z))["X"]    # Y on X and Z
```

When you own the program you can check a claim about $do(\cdot)$
directly: replace the line for $X$ by a constant and run the lines
below it again.

```{r ovb_do}
Y_do1 <- 0.5 * 1 + 1 * Z + rnorm(n)     # everyone gets X = 1; Z untouched
Y_do0 <- 0.5 * 0 + 1 * Z + rnorm(n)     # everyone gets X = 0
mean(Y_do1) - mean(Y_do0)
```

Repeating the first simulation 200 times at each of four sample sizes
shows the difference between bias and variance. Both estimates vary
less as the sample grows. The slope of $Y$ on $X$ alone settles on 1.0,
and the coefficient from the fit with $Z$ settles on the effect, 0.5.

```{r ovb_sizes, fig.height=3.2}
one_sample <- function(n) {
  Z <- rnorm(n)
  X <- Z + rnorm(n)
  Y <- 0.5 * X + Z + rnorm(n)
  c(coef(lm(Y ~ X))[2], coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z))[2])
}
sims <- bind_rows(lapply(c(50, 200, 1000, 5000), function(n) {
  est <- replicate(200, one_sample(n))      # 2 rows, 200 columns
  data.frame(n = n, slope = c(est[1, ], est[2, ]),
             fit = rep(c("Y on X alone", "Y on X and Z"), each = 200))
}))
ggplot(sims, aes(factor(n), slope, color = fit)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.5, 1), linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = two, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "sample size", y = "coefficient on X")
```

## Unobserved confounding

The adjustment formula needs every back door blocked, and the graph that
says which back doors exist is drawn by the analyst. For the job-search
course I put one variable behind the referral. A colleague could put
two: work last year, $Z$, and something unmeasured, $U$, say
motivation, which also pushes people onto the course and into work. The
reading draws such variables with dashed arrows.

```{r unobs_dag, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.4, fig.width=3}
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("Z", "U", "X", "Y"), x = c(0.4, 1.6, 0, 2), y = c(1.1, 1.1, 0, 0)),
         data.frame(from = c("Z", "Z", "U", "U", "X"), to = c("X", "Y", "X", "Y", "Y")),
         dashed = c("U X", "U Y"))
```

Under my graph, adjusting for $Z$ gives the effect, 10 points. Under
the colleague's graph the back door through $U$ is still open. If $U$
pushes people both onto the course and into work, as motivation would,
the 10 points is likely to overstate the effect, and the data cannot
say by how much. The data on $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are the same under both
graphs, and fit both. To decide between them you need arguments about
what sends people onto the course and what helps them find work, and
regression output will not supply them.

A randomized trial is the case where the analyst knows what decided
who was assigned the treatment, because the analyst decided it: the
arrow into the assignment comes from a coin, so the comparison of the
arms has no back door, measured or not. That is why the hormone trial
was taken to settle a question that many adjusted observational
estimates had not. Most policies cannot be tried that way first. Then
the graph is an argument, and a consequentialist's case for the policy
stands or falls with it.

## Reinforcement learning

**Notation:** this section uses the letters of reinforcement learning:
$S$ state, $A$ action, $R$ reward, $\pi$ policy, $U$ utility.

An agent observes a **state** $S$, takes an **action** $A$, and receives
a **reward** $R$. A **policy** $\pi$ is a rule that chooses the action
from the state, $A = \pi(S)$, and learning means changing the policy to
make the expected reward, $E_\pi[R]$, large, where $E_\pi$ is the
expectation when the agent acts by $\pi$. The **utility** $U$ is what
we care about. A utilitarian would choose the policy whose
expected utility $E_\pi[U]$ is largest. The agent is given $R$ instead,
because $R$ can be measured and $U$ often cannot: in the job center
below, $U$ needs what would have happened without the course. $R$ and
$U$ can come apart.

```{r rl_loop, echo=FALSE, fig.height=1.7, fig.width=6, dev.args=list(symbolfamily=grDevices::cairoSymbolFont("MathJax_Math", usePUA=FALSE)), fig.alt="A loop: the agent, with policy pi, sends an action A to the environment, which returns a state S and a reward R to the agent."}
# dev.args draws pi in MathJax_Math, the TeX italic of an older MathJax, so that it looks
# like the pi in the formulas. Where that font is missing, the system substitutes another.
loop_boxes <- data.frame(x = c(0, 3), y = c(0, 0), label = c("atop(agent, policy~pi)", "environment"))
loop_top <- data.frame(x = 0.62, y = 0.28, xend = 2.28, yend = 0.28)
loop_bottom <- data.frame(x = 2.28, y = -0.28, xend = 0.62, yend = -0.28)
loop_text <- data.frame(x = c(1.45, 1.45), y = c(1.12, -1.12),
                        label = c("action $A$", "state $S$, reward $R$"))
ggplot() +
  geom_curve(data = loop_top, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend), curvature = -0.35,
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed"), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_curve(data = loop_bottom, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend), curvature = -0.35,
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed"), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_label(data = loop_boxes, aes(x, y, label = label), parse = TRUE, size = 4.5,
             label.padding = unit(0.5, "lines")) +
  geom_mathtext(data = loop_text, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 4.2) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.9, 3.9), ylim = c(-1.3, 1.3)) +
  theme_void()
```

Amodei and colleagues (2016) use a cleaning robot as a running example.
In these letters, the state is what the robot's camera shows, the
actions are where to move and whether to clean, and the utility is a
clean room. If the reward is for not seeing any mess, the robot can
earn it by closing its eyes, or by covering the mess with something it
cannot see through.

```{r robot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.3, fig.width=7, fig.alt="Three rooms, each earning reward 1. Left: the robot cleans, and its view shows no mess. Middle: it closes its eyes, and the mess stays. Right: it covers the mess, which stays under the cover."}
panels <- c("cleans", "closes its eyes", "covers the mess")
room <- data.frame(panel = factor(panels, levels = panels))
cone <- do.call(rbind, lapply(panels[c(1, 3)], function(p)
  data.frame(panel = p, x = c(2.6, 9.6, 9.6), y = c(2.3, 7.4, 3.0))))
mess <- data.frame(panel = rep(panels[2:3], each = 2), x = c(7.6, 8.4, 7.6, 8.4), y = c(5.0, 4.3, 5.0, 4.3))
cover <- data.frame(panel = panels[3], xmin = 6.5, xmax = 9.7, ymin = 3.2, ymax = 6.1)
caption <- data.frame(panel = panels, x = 5, y = -1.6,
                      label = c("$R$ = 1, room clean", "$R$ = 1, room dirty", "$R$ = 1, room dirty"))
for (d in c("cone", "mess", "cover", "caption")) {
  z <- get(d); z$panel <- factor(z$panel, levels = panels); assign(d, z)
}
ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = room, aes(xmin = 0, xmax = 10, ymin = 0, ymax = 8), fill = NA, color = slate, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_polygon(data = cone, aes(x, y), fill = gold, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = mess, aes(x, y), size = 5, color = khaki) +
  geom_rect(data = cover, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax), fill = cgray, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = data.frame(x = 2, y = 2), aes(x, y), size = 6, color = navy) +
  geom_mathtext(data = caption, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-0.3, 10.3), ylim = c(-2.4, 8.3)) +
  theme_void() + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 11), panel.spacing = unit(1.2, "lines"))
```

Now a variant of the job center, with 100 places on the course, which
helps some people more than others. Of people who worked last year, 70% are in work six months
later if they take the course and 64% if they do not; of people who did
not work last year, 40% and 14%. The state is a person's record, the
action is to refer or not, and the center is judged on the share of
the people it refers who are in work, its placement rate. That rate is
its reward. Referring 100 people who worked last year earns a rate of
70% and puts 6 more people in work, on average, than would be in work
without the course. Referring 100 who did not earns 40% and puts 26 more
in work. A center judged on its placement rate refers the first group;
a utilitarian counting the jobs the course creates refers the second,
and so serves the people who need the course most.

```{r skim, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.2, fig.width=6, fig.alt="Two panels of invented numbers for the variant job center. Placement rate: 70 percent if it sends people who worked last year, 40 percent if it sends those who did not. Extra people in work: 6 against 26."}
skim <- data.frame(group = factor(rep(c("worked last year", "did not"), 2), levels = c("worked last year", "did not")),
                   panel = factor(rep(c("R", "U"), each = 2), levels = c("R", "U")),
                   value = c(70, 40, 6, 26), shown = c("70%", "40%", "6", "26"))
# the panels' titles, drawn above the panels by geom_mathtext so that R and U are in the
# formulas' italic (a strip's text has one font)
titles <- data.frame(panel = factor(c("R", "U"), levels = c("R", "U")), x = 1.5, y = Inf,
                     label = c("$R$: placement rate", "$U$: extra people in work"))
ggplot(skim, aes(group, value, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = shown), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.8) +
  geom_mathtext(data = titles, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 8.8 / .pt, colour = "grey10",
                vjust = 0, nudge_y = 4.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = two) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.3))) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "the 100 people sent", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(t = 18, r = 5.5, b = 5.5, l = 5.5))
```

Choosing people who would have done well anyway is called cream
skimming. Heckman, Heinrich and Smith (2002) studied it in US
job-training centers funded under the Job Training Partnership Act,
which were judged partly on employment rates. They found the short-run
measures "weakly, and sometimes perversely, related to long run
impacts." They also found that cream skimming made little difference
to the programs' efficiency, in either direction, unlike the invented
numbers above, and concluded: "Opposition to cream skimming must come
on equity grounds." Equity here is about who is served; efficiency is
about the total.

Each of the four difficulties of utilitarianism becomes a choice
someone makes in building such an agent. Defining utility becomes
choosing $R$, a measurable stand-in for $U$, and in both examples the
two come apart. Trading off between people becomes adding the reward up
over the people the agent serves; the placement rate counts only the
people referred. Judging acts or rules becomes choosing a policy, a
rule that treats alike everyone in the same state. Judging each action
on its own and judging the rule can give different answers: when a rule
has to treat different situations alike, as a model that sees only a
few variables about each person does; when places are limited, so that
one referral uses a place another person could have had; and when
people respond to the rule itself. Predicting consequences becomes
choosing a model of what the actions do, which is a causal model.

Is $E_\pi[U]$ a causal quantity? It can be read as one, the expected
utility if the agent's actions were set by $\pi$, but that reading
needs assumptions beyond this week's. An intervention in this week's
sense sets a variable for everyone in a population. Here one agent
follows a rule. The people and systems it acts on may respond to what
it does, sometimes adversarially, and what happens to one of them can
depend on what was done to others. Causal reinforcement learning, a
subfield surveyed by Deng, Jiang, Long and Zhang (2023), brings causal
models into reinforcement learning.

These letters clash with the ones used for prediction, which most of
the course uses.

| | prediction | reinforcement learning |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $A$ | sensitive attribute: something a person *is* | action: something an agent *does* |
| $R$ | risk score, with $\hat Y = 1\{R \ge t\}$ | reward |
| $U$ | unobserved variable | utility |
| $S$, $\pi$ | not used | state, policy |

If you read about reinforcement learning you will meet these letters
with these meanings. New letters invented for this course would teach a
convention nobody else uses. Two rules are enough. Material that uses
the reinforcement-learning letters says so in one line at the top, as
this section does. And the two sets of letters are never mixed inside
one diagram or one derivation. A classifier described as an agent takes
its prediction $\hat Y$ as its action, which reinforcement learning
would write as $A$. Mixing the two there would give $A$ two meanings in
one line.

## An argument in prose

A council says: "Pupils who go to their school's breakfast club have
better attendance and better test results. We will fund a breakfast
club in each of our schools, because breakfast clubs improve results."
The argument assumes a graph, and drawing it shows what evidence the
council would need.

```{r club_dag, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.4, fig.width=7}
draw_dag(data.frame(name = c("funding", "goes to the club", "attendance", "test results", "family circumstances"),
                    x = c(-0.9, 0.5, 1.45, 2.45, 1.45), y = c(0.6, 0.6, -0.05, 0.6, 1.3)),
         data.frame(from = c("funding", "goes to the club", "goes to the club", "attendance",
                             "family circumstances", "family circumstances"),
                    to = c("goes to the club", "attendance", "test results", "test results",
                           "goes to the club", "test results")),
         boxes = TRUE, xlim = c(-1.6, 3.3), ylim = c(-0.3, 1.55))
```

The council's action is funding, which changes whether a school has a
club. Its evidence compares pupils who go with pupils who do not, and
nobody chose who goes by tossing a coin. Family circumstances can
affect both whether a pupil goes and how the pupil does at school, so
they open a back door. Attendance is a mediator, one route by which
going could improve results. A comparison that matches the action is
schools with a club against schools without one, and the strongest
version is a trial in which some schools are given a club at random.

## Lenses

What are we optimizing or predicting? The job center optimizes its
placement rate, not the jobs the course creates, and the cleaning robot
what its camera shows, not the room.

Which comparison gets reported? Attenders against non-attenders, or
attenders against non-attenders within each row of the table. Women who
took hormones against women who did not, or women who started against
women who did not, followed from the same day. In each pair the first
comparison comes with the data, and the second is the one an action
needs. In the course table the first is nearly three times the second.
In the hormone studies the first gave 0.39, and the second gave 1.42
over the first two years (interval 0.92 to 2.20) and 0.96 over the
whole follow-up (0.78 to 1.18), estimates the authors call similar to
the trial's. And the average effect, or the effects within groups
defined before treatment. The first is all a utilitarian choosing
between everyone and no one needs; the second is closer to what the
Belmont principle of justice asks about.

You have to choose, so choose, and defend it. "Pretending it was forced
is its own failure." Which variables to adjust for follows from a graph,
and you drew the graph. A colleague can draw another that fits the same
numbers. The backdoor criterion narrows the choice. Given a graph, it
tells you which sets are valid. Drawing the graph is up to you.
Declining to draw one does not remove the choice. The argument you are
reading has usually drawn it already, as "$X$ causes $Y$", without
saying so.

And why? The observational comparison comes free with the data. The
interventional one needs a graph, and a graph is an argument that
someone can attack. Whoever is making the case for a policy has a reason
to prefer the first.

## For the class

### Effects that differ between groups

In the course table, attending adds 10 points in both rows. Effects can
differ between rows, and then the average treatment effect depends on
how common each row is. If the within-row effects were $0.06$ for
$Z = 1$ and $0.26$ for $Z = 0$, the average treatment effect would be
$0.06\,P(Z = 1) + 0.26\,P(Z = 0)$: $0.16$ when the rows are equal in
size, and $0.08$ in a population where 90% have $Z = 1$. The
reading calls such effects heterogeneous. An average treatment effect
belongs to a population, so before you carry one to a new population,
ask whether the two have the same mix.

A decision is usually a change from what happens now, not a choice
between everyone and no one. Sending everyone to the course changes
$X$ only for the 500 people who did not attend, 100 with $Z = 1$ and
400 with $Z = 0$. With the effects above, the overall rate would rise
by $(100 \times 0.06 + 400 \times 0.26)/1000 = 0.11$. That is the
effect among the people who did not attend, $0.22$, times their share,
one half. The average treatment effect, $0.16$, compares everyone
attending with nobody attending, which is a different question.
Outside this example, offering the course to everyone would not make
everyone attend.

### More than one adjustment set

A graph can allow more than one valid adjustment set. Add to the course
graph a variable $W$ with an arrow into $Y$ and no other arrows, such as
the distance from a person's home to the nearest large employer. $W$ is
on no backdoor path, so $\{Z\}$ and $\{Z, W\}$ are both valid, and in a
linear model the coefficient on $X$ converges to $\beta$ either way.
The choice between them is about variance, not bias. Adding $W$ removes
some of the unexplained variation in $Y$, so the estimate from
$\{Z, W\}$ is usually less variable.
